newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria poll fuels speculation on Abacha candidacy.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria poll fuels speculation on Abacha candidacy.

text.p: Supporters of Nigeria's military leader Sani Abacha took a commanding lead on Monday in local elections, fuelling speculation that the general labelled a dictator by Western critics will seek to legitimise his rule through the ballot box.
The political camp leading the campaign to draft Abacha as candidate for presidential elections next year to end army rule swept town halls, including bastions of opposition to Abacha.

In the latest results on Monday the pro-Abacha United Nigeria Congress Party (UNCP) even won comfortably in the home state of Moshood Abiola, who has been in detention since declaring himself head of state after claiming victory in elections in 1994.
The UNCP took 13 local council chairmanships of the 19 declared in Abiola's southwestern Ogun state, according to latest results from provincial electoral authorities published in newspapers.

Nationwide the UNCP swept 177 chairmanships in the 24 of the country's 36 states where results were available. Second, with 105 chairmanships was the Democratic Party of Nigeria, which has also declared its willingess to support Abacha for president.
The three other legal parties managed only a combined 96 chairmanships.
"Those two (leading) parties have been generally perceived as the government parties," said a Western diplomat monitoring Abacha's programme to restore democracy in the unstable nation.

"It is clear that nobody wants to be on the losing side. Everything is now pointing in the direction of an Abacha candidacy and people believe the UNCP is his party," said a Lagos-based Nigerian lawyer who asked not to be named.
The military government cited peaceful voting on Saturday as proof of popular support for Abacha's plan, criticised by the West as too slow, to transfer power to civilians next year.

The UNCP strength in centres of opposition to Abacha, notably Lagos and Abiola's home region, surprised many political analysts. Pro-democracy campaigners said it showed Abacha's government had succeeded in stamping out credible opposition.
Several leading opposition figures are in prison or exile. Many of Nigeria's most experienced and influential politicians ignored the elections because their parties were not registered.

Political analysts said that with results of the local elections redefining the Nigerian political landscape, the opposition figures are expected to rejoin the fray, raising the prospect of a changed scenario in future elections.
State elections are due later this year, with national and presidential polls scheduled for next year to wrap up the transition to civilian rule.
Abacha seized power in 1993 after previous army rulers aborted a plan to return Nigeria to civil rule, sparking unrest.
He ignored pressure at home and from the West for an early return to democracy and pressed on with his own civil-rule plan. Saturday's poll was the first on party lines since 1993.
Pro-democracy activists say they believe Abacha will follow a growing band of military strongmen in West Africa who have legitimised their rule through carefully controlled elections.

Abacha's only comment is that it depends on his "constituency". He has not stated if the constituency is the army or another group but supporters say he is as free as anyone to contest elections once he quits the army.
Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro said the orderly and enthusiastic voting showed that Nigerians endorsed the government's transition programme.
